item.title: Clice v1.0 Released: Welcome to Modern C++ (135 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ykiko.me/en/articles/2105384023094834022/, See on Hacker News

clice recently hit 1,000 commits, a special milestone for the project. Since July 19, 2026, clice has been shipping nightly builds and going through roughly four months of alpha testing, with a huge number of bugs fixed thanks to real-world feedback from early users. Over the same stretch, I built a rigorous testing system for clice and ran extensive tests across many real open-source projects, tracking down and fixing the issues they uncovered. What does that mean? Every core feature is now stable, and you rarely run into problems in day-to-day use. So I think the time is right to ship the first stable release. The project looks very different today from where it stood two years ago in Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, and this is probably the first time I’m promoting it widely, so please let me introduce it to you once again! This is the project I have poured the past two and a half years into, the work I am proudest of, the one that has excited me the most and left me sad and anxious more times than I can count, and the most ambitious thing I have taken on in my short life.

What is clice?

In short, clice is a C/C++ language server written in modern C++, but it’s more than just a language server. It is still built on LLVM/Clang, but unlike clangd and ccls, which are also Clang-based, clice was redesigned from the ground up to fix architectural problems that have gone unsolved in those servers for years. It is written entirely in C++23 and serves as an example of modern C++ best practices in its own right, with all the major modern C++ features coming together remarkably well:

  • Written entirely with C++20 coroutines, using our own libuv-based structured-concurrency async library for intricate asynchronous logic. It is a complex concurrent program running an event loop on the main thread while coordinating both multiple processes (IPC) and multiple threads.
  • Written entirely with C++20 named modules and C++23 import std, and fully self-hosted: module wrappers for third-party libraries are generated automatically by clice modularize, and clice runs smoothly on its own codebase to provide module-aware language services.
  • Uses static reflection built on templates and C++20 concepts for all serialization and deserialization across formats, including TOML, JSON, bincode, blob, and command-line arguments, with Rust-macro-like declarative annotations and zero boilerplate.
  • Data-oriented code design throughout, with almost no virtual functions outside the callback interfaces Clang requires. Makes heavy use of modern C++ APIs like std::format, std::expected, std::ranges, and std::views, steering clear of outdated legacy C++98/11 APIs.
  • A completely hermetic, reproducible build powered by Bazel, compiled with the unified xclang toolchain for a consistent cross-platform cross-compilation workflow. Compiled binaries are heavily optimized (PGO + LTO), and build artifacts depend on nothing beyond system libraries.

People are always debating whether modern C++ features like modules are actually ready for real work. clice’s answer is: yes, of course, completely usable! They hold up for complex software like clice, with hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Maybe this is what the modern C++ we have been hoping for looks like. That said, the surrounding ecosystem really is inconvenient enough right now that getting this whole workflow running end to end took a huge amount of effort on my part to track issues and adapt everything.

Language Server

Here is an overview of clice’s main features:

  • Multi-process compilation: clice compiles code in a process pool modeled after modern web browsers, whereas clangd uses multithreading. Why multiple processes? Because C++ is simply too complex, and on certain corner cases the compiler can easily crash or leak memory. That is especially true for incomplete code in the middle of editing: a huge downstream user base tests compilers on complete code, while very few people test them on half-written code, where the compiler mostly falls back on best-effort heuristics. In clangd, a compiler crash takes down the whole server and forces a restart. In clice, compilation happens in isolated child processes: losing one worker does not affect the rest of the server, so go-to-definition, highlighting, and other services keep working. It also makes it much easier to manage memory usage and schedule compilation priorities, cutting down on unnecessary resource consumption.

  • Modules and shared caching: clice has full support for C++20 named modules. All you need is a compile_commands.json containing all module files, and clice scans dependencies on its own and lazily builds required modules on demand, regardless of your build system or compiler, with full support for module completion, highlighting, go-to-definition, hover, and more. Built PCHs and PCMs are also cached on local disk for reuse across sessions. By comparison, clangd offers only very limited module support and no persistent cache.

  • Compilation context: clice has full support for non-self-contained files, and more generally for the concept of a compilation context. You can explicitly pick the active context of a file: a specific compile command for a source file, or a specific inclusion site for a header. When you open a non-self-contained file, clice detects its context automatically, so it works out of the box. More broadly, it also supports grouping compile commands into build configurations, letting you switch between, say, debug and release.

  • Better template support: clice implements a DFS pseudo instantiator that infers what many dependent names resolve to without needing concrete template arguments for a full instantiation. When a template has been instantiated once, clice also draws on that instantiation to power language features, such as completing on auto parameters of a lambda passed to a ranges call. On top of that, clice treats a template as a duck-typed interface and each instantiation as one of its implementations, much like a virtual function and its overrides: Go to Implementation on a dependent call inside a template lists the functions it actually calls across every instantiation, and Find References and Call Hierarchy work the same way.

  • Out-of-the-box experience: Most projects need nothing more than a compile_commands.json. clice ships with built-in environment probing for 50+ toolchains, covering nvcc, MSYS2, Cygwin, zigcc, and more, automatically handling mismatches between your actual compiler and Clang. You don’t have to manually add piles of compiler flags to a config file the way you do with clangd.

Beyond these main features, clice also fixes a long list of smaller clangd issues that have gone untouched for years across semantic highlighting, folding, hover, and more. If you’re interested, give it a try and see what surprises you find. Overall, clice surpasses clangd in ease of use, feature support, and performance. You can install the clice extension in VS Code and other editors and start using it right now.

Command Line

Besides running as a language server, clice can also be used from the CLI to access its language features directly. Currently supported subcommands include:

  • clice index: Builds a persistent index for the entire project ahead of time and supports resuming interrupted runs, so your editor starts warm as soon as you open the project.
  • clice lint: Built-in clang-tidy runner that checks translation units concurrently across a process pool and merges duplicate diagnostics from headers; pass --index to reuse the same parse pass to build the index along the way.
  • clice format: A wrapper around clang-format that automatically finds files to format from your config file or CDB and formats them efficiently in parallel.
  • clice command: Shows the effective compile command for a file after rule rewrites and toolchain probing, or converts compile_commands.json into resolved -cc1 commands for other Clang tools.
  • clice query: Reads the on-disk index directly without starting a server and outputs symbol definitions, references, call graphs, inheritance hierarchies, and file dependencies as JSON.
  • clice refactor: Rewrites source files directly from the persistent index without recompiling, supporting project-wide symbol and macro renaming as well as batch renames in one pass via --spec.
  • clice analyze: Outputs project-structure JSON from the index to guide refactoring; for example, analyze modules analyzes module dependencies and cycles across directories and lists code patterns that stand in the way of modularization.
  • clice modularize: Automatically wraps third-party libraries used by a project as C++20 modules without modifying any source files; following the split analyze proposes, it can also rewrite the project’s own code into module units, turning headers into partitions and #include into import. clice used it to modularize itself.

The story behind it

That wraps up the feature tour. Next, I want to talk about the story behind the project, some of its design decisions, and my own thoughts and struggles along the way, especially now, in the age of AI.

Why not improve clangd?

First, why start a new project instead of improving clangd? That is the question I get asked most often. There are several reasons. I discussed some of them in my earliest post, and today those problems are even easier to see firsthand:

  • Maintenance and staffing: At root, clangd has been effectively unmaintained since around 2024. That sounds surprising. How could a tool used by hundreds of thousands of developers have no one maintaining it? I stumbled onto this fact in 2024 when I was getting ready to submit a PR to clangd for better code completion inside templates. From what I understand, it ties back to a shift in Google’s C++ strategy. Before that, clangd was maintained mainly by several Google engineers, and around 2024 Google started scaling back its investment in C++ (Clang); clangd was deemed good enough for Google’s internal needs, and those engineers were reassigned elsewhere. Since then, clangd has lacked any real long-term maintainers. Only Nathan Ridge has been answering questions unpaid in his spare time, purely out of passion, and one person only has so much bandwidth, making it nearly impossible to handle large PRs. That is why clangd’s C++20 modules PR dragged on for nearly a year, and even today it still isn’t really usable on large projects, with plenty of flaws and nobody working on them. Earlier this year, in 2026, Clang’s lead maintainer Aaron Ballman recognized the problem and posted a call for help on the community forum, saying clangd is very close to unmaintained, with a heavy backlog of PRs and issues, and hoping to find new community maintainers; otherwise clangd could eventually be removed from the LLVM project.

  • Scale of the code changes: As mentioned at the start, clice introduces many new architectural ideas, such as multi-process compilation. Implementing those inside clangd would come close to rewriting clangd. Nobody is going to review and accept changes of that size. Self-hosting with modules would also require sweeping changes to LLVM’s build system, which I will go into in detail when I introduce xclang later.

  • LLVM repository constraints: clice relies on a lot of third-party libraries for better performance and user experience, such as libuv, simdjson, and tomlplusplus. To keep builds simple, LLVM requires the repository to remain self-contained, so pulling in that many third-party libraries is out of the question. You would either have to rewrite and port them into LLVM or put up with worse ergonomics and lower performance. On top of that, a language server is not a standalone project: it also includes extensions and adapters for different editors. Keeping them in the same repo as the server makes maintenance much easier, and LLVM would be just as unlikely to accept that editor code (spanning Rust, Lua, TypeScript, and so on). For long-term maintainability and our core goals, a separate repository was unavoidable.

So in mid-2024, I started looking into how to design and write a new language server. At the end of 2024, I published Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, setting out clice’s core goals and kicking off development in earnest.

How did we get here?

Next, let’s talk about how clice was built. How did it get to its current state? Over the past two and a half years, at a rough guess, I have put nearly 3,000 hours into this project. Even that number doesn’t really tell the story, because clice became part of my life. It was always on my mind, like eating or sleeping: there wasn’t a moment when I wasn’t turning over some problem related to it. Development broke down into roughly four stages:

Mid-2024 to early 2025: I spent this period studying Clang and clangd’s codebase and internals. Anyone who has looked through my older blog posts will know I am a longtime template metaprogramming enthusiast, familiar with C++ and its implementation details down to language-lawyer territory. During this phase I settled on clice’s core goals and overall design, and put together an initial demo. I was a third-year undergrad at the time: I would wake up and start coding right away, skip lunch, walk out to the McDonald’s outside the campus gate when I got hungry, and put in 8 to 10 hours a day.

Early 2025 to early 2026: I originally expected to ship a usable version of clice fairly quickly during this stage. Instead, progress went much slower than I expected, and it remained a long way from production-ready. Looking back, there were a few main reasons:

  1. Above all, time. I had assumed I would keep putting in 8 to 10 hours a day like before. My undergraduate major was chemistry, though, and everything I knew about programming was self-taught. Even though I had plenty of C++ experience and had participated in GSoC, I lacked specific “domain knowledge.” To find a job, I spent most of 2025 interning and picking up a new field (unrelated to C++ frontends), while also dealing with university chores and everything involved in graduating. The hours I had left for clice shrank drastically compared to my earlier assumptions, so progress naturally slowed down.
  2. Getting the project genuinely production-ready also took far more than the core architecture. It meant working through countless corner cases of C++ syntax alongside subtle cross-platform differences: URI parsing, file paths and file uniqueness, OS-level quirks, and so on. The workload turned out to be much bigger than I had imagined. I also have a bit of an obsessive streak and dislike band-aid solutions that barely get by, so to build things the way I wanted I ended up reinventing quite a few wheels, covering serialization, IPC/LSP, async, and more. Had I chosen Rust at the start, development might have taken considerably less time, since those pieces already existed in the Rust ecosystem and had been thoroughly proven in other language servers. Still, writing a C++ language server in Rust felt odd, and it would have ruled out self-hosting, so I didn’t go that route.
  3. Lack of experience scheduling and managing complex software. Even with so much work on the table, several early contributors were already interested in the project and willing to put real time into helping write code. Unfortunately, I had very little teamwork experience back then (being completely self-taught and only three years into programming altogether), so I failed to turn that interest into effective contributions. That sank in much deeper once I started working in industry: 3 or 4 of my coworkers can split up responsibilities, stand up a project from scratch in 2 to 3 months, and ship it to production, whereas I had poor instincts for project planning and mostly just wrote whatever was on my mind at the moment. Open-source volunteer bandwidth can’t be compared to a full-time job, of course, yet the truth is I didn’t do a great job of building a community or pushing the project forward.

Early 2026 to July 2026: The turning point came when coding agents led by Claude Opus 4.6 started catching on. I began using agents to help with the mountain of tedious detail work and painful cross-platform debugging, and found they were remarkably good at it. During this stretch I did a sweeping cleanup of the existing codebase and established the prototype of clice as it stands today. As agents grew stronger, I handed them increasingly complex tasks and kept moving the project forward rapidly. It was an exciting period: I could finally stop burning hours on tedious details and focus on architecture and feature work. At the same time, it hit me that coding agents were only going to keep getting stronger. If humans stop writing code altogether in the future, what point does a language server even have? That pushed me to start designing and building clice’s CLI features.

July 2026 to present: By July I felt the timing was right to put out early test builds and iterate based on real user feedback. Core language server features were already in place and fully usable day to day, though still short of everything I had originally envisioned, so I threw myself into building out the rest of that vision, tuning performance, and fixing bugs. In October, I started planning clice’s modular self-hosting. That was a remarkably complicated undertaking, because C++ module support today is a long, painful story:

  • CMake supports modules, yet if implementation units importing a module use different compile flags, CMake forks a separate compilation of the module even when those flags don’t affect PCM compatibility. CMake also has no built-in compilation cache, which matters a lot for CI; normally we reach for ccache to solve that, except ccache doesn’t support modules.
  • clice has a demanding platform matrix: six combinations across Windows/Linux/macOS × ARM64/x64, plus ASan builds, prebuilt LLVM/Clang binaries to speed up CI, C++23 import std, and build artifacts that depend only on system libraries rather than extra shared libraries so everything works out of the box for users.

I surveyed the options extensively, and the answer was that an out-of-the-box setup for this simply did not exist in open source, and most open-source C++ module projects don’t have build requirements nearly this involved. After thinking it through carefully, I built xclang, inspired by zigcc, to give every target platform a unified cross-compilation experience, and paired it with Bazel (which includes built-in build caching) to solve the build problem for good. Going one step further, I wrote clice modularize to automatically generate module wrappers for every third-party library we depend on, completing clice’s self-hosted modularization! That probably makes clice one of the most complex open-source C++ projects using modules today.

Alongside all of this, I ran extensive fuzz testing across many open-source projects and fixed a huge number of bugs, bringing clice to genuine production readiness!

What about agents?

As I mentioned earlier, I designed a CLI interface for clice so that it would still hold some value in the agent era. An obvious idea is replacing grep with clice query: it is more accurate and uses fewer tokens. That is true, except exact symbol lookup requires indexing the whole project first, which takes a very long time. grep is imprecise, sure, yet 2 or 3 grep calls are usually enough to find the target, and the extra text grep pulls back isn’t necessarily a bad thing for helping an agent understand the codebase. Put plainly, most of this CLI isn’t actually all that useful. The part that really earns its keep is probably clice modularize: if you ask an agent to modularize a project on its own, it spins up a swarm of subagents and writes custom scripts to pull off the migration, which is both slow and expensive. Giving the agent clice modularize to assist the migration works much better. LLMs are trained first and foremost for generality, and what they do best is writing and combining scripts to generalize across problems. As things stand, only highly specialized tools still carry real value; otherwise you are usually better off letting the LLM compose its own scripts.

As agents keep getting stronger, especially with models led by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the cost of building complex software keeps falling, and 10x or even 100x the productivity of the past is well within reach. Over on X, you can see plenty of people asking Claude in a single sentence to rewrite the TypeScript compiler in another programming language and getting better performance out of it. Surprising at first glance, yet completely reasonable when you think about it. Software written in the past was bounded by human time, cost, and skill, so codebases inevitably accumulated lots of suboptimal code paths. When humans optimize performance, we go after the main bottlenecks, whereas an agent can tirelessly optimize every path until the small wins add up. Refactoring also often produces a better architecture than existing code; rewriting or refactoring software was just too expensive to justify before. In the foreseeable future, then, most code may be written entirely by agents, humans may stop writing code and even reading it (which is already happening now), and language servers may have no reason to exist at all. Agents might even invent programming languages better suited to themselves: compilation and interpretation themselves have often become the bottleneck in the agent loop, and agents already have the ability to optimize that underlying infrastructure; they just haven’t started yet. Ideally, every stage of the agent loop should be something the agent itself can improve and speed up, compilers and toolchains included.

To be continued

That is a sad reality, and in an era like this it means the effort I poured into clice over the past two and a half years is unlikely to have the lasting meaning I first imagined. Every time I dwell on it, I slip into a dark mood, bordering on nihilism. I can’t help asking myself: thousands of hours and a lot of money, and what was it all for?

Because I taught myself programming off the beaten path without a CS degree, I got used early on to the cycle of finding my own goals, defining problems, solving them, and then looking for the next goal. Interest alone only sustains me for a little while; sticking with something for the long haul takes some deeper “meaning” or “vision” behind it, ideally one I defined for myself. And now that meaning is fading away. So over the past few months, I started pushing myself relentlessly. The more those thoughts crept in, the harder I used agents to drive the project forward, trying to finish it before it lost its meaning altogether.

Imagine an alternate timeline where coding agents never took off. clice wouldn’t be nearly as complete as it is today, of course, yet I would have slowly gained experience, learned how to collaborate and plan work, built a community around it, and watched clice move forward slowly and steadily. Except the SOTA models have already been trained. Models like Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are real, and whether AI is a bubble or not, they aren’t going away. Software becoming cheap is already an undeniable fact.

We have to face reality, so what mindset should we bring to all of this? My thinking has shifted again recently, though honestly neither my mental state nor my daily life is in a great place right now. Pouring yourself too deeply into one thing naturally takes a heavy toll when it doesn’t turn out the way you hoped. Still, if you zoom out over a longer stretch of time, what does it really amount to? Even if I had done nothing at all for these two and a half years, so what? There is plenty of life ahead. I know that in principle, yet letting go is hard, especially when this project has been part of my life for over two years. As I mentioned in an earlier post, graduating from college never really felt real to me, because the rhythm of my life barely changed afterward: apart from my job, it was just this project. Something has to change eventually, though. I can treat clice as my graduation project: my real graduation project, not one from the chemistry major I never really liked. And that’s enough. I don’t need to force a grander meaning onto it. This graduation project has met every single goal I set two years ago, and exceeded them by a wide margin. It stands on its own as the best illustration of modern C++, neatly bringing together everything I studied about C++ in college. If on top of that it can be helpful to people just learning to program or curious about modern C++, that is plenty.

So this post is a kind of ritual for me. I need to step out of my old life and look for other things worth doing, maybe things outside code. I will keep maintaining clice, just not at the intensity I used to; practically everything worth building is already built anyway, so from here on it will mostly be incremental optimizations and bug fixes based on user feedback. In times like these, it is hard to say what the right path is, or what you ought to be doing. Nobody knows what will happen next week, let alone next year, or how far AI will actually go. I think it is time to rest for a while so I don’t burn out, and have the energy to face whatever problems come next. I still have a strong drive to keep creating good work. It just might not be about programming anymore, and figuring that out is what I need to learn and think through in this next stage.

That’s all for this post. Thanks for reading. I hope you’ll give clice a try, and feel free to report any problems!

item.title: 'Duffy Lied': Controllers Refute Transportation Secretary's Ground Stop Story (153 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.commondreams.org/news/duffy-ground-stop-explanation, See on Hacker News

Air traffic controllers are rejecting US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation for Friday's nationwide flight ground stop, raising questions about the Trump administration's account of a communications failure that disrupted air travel across the United States, affecting an estimated 1.5 million travelers.

Washington Examiner homeland security reporter Anna Giaritelli told CNN's Laura Coates during a Friday night interview that she'd spoken with 60 air traffic controllers about the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, which was just the third to ever occur.

"None of them are buying what he said," Giaritelli said. "The controllers were saying, 'We don’t buy that this is actually what’s happening, the reason that Sean Duffy is saying this has happened.'"

At a White House briefing Friday evening, Duffy blamed the disruption on America's aging air traffic control infrastructure, saying overloaded switches and routers had produced inconsistent radar and communications data.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data,” he said. “And because of that, we shut the system down.”

But Giaritelli said the controllers she contacted questioned the plausibility of the administration's account, particularly the timing of the alleged equipment changes.

“These types of switches... that the FAA is doing, they don't happen during the day,” she told Coates. “They don't happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They're doing these midweek, middle of the night, when there is no air traffic going on."

Giaritelli's comments came as the Trump administration struggled to explain how a failure in the nation's air traffic control network could have escalated into a shutdown affecting airports nationwide. The FAA lifted the ground stop at approximately 8:15 pm Eastern on Friday, but the disruption continued Saturday.

Duffy offered a new detail on Saturday, saying that a system overload occurred when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire.

“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” the secretary said, adding that officials were investigating whether the contractor's "incompetence" or a faulty router was to blame.

Duffy emphatically denied that the FAA's recent nationwide rollout of an $875 million artificial intelligence system called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) had anything to do with Friday's disruption, claiming that the system "is not even plugged in."

The FAA said earlier this week that it "will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 [air traffic control] centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption, and improve the travel experience for the flying public."

Duffy also used the crisis to renew his demand for $50 billion in congressional funding to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system, arguing that the aging infrastructure would continue to fail without additional investment.

The administration's shifting account has added to calls for an independent investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday that investigators had found no evidence of a cyberattack, although he acknowledged that the possibility had not been entirely ruled out.

Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) was among those who challenged the administration's explanation, suggesting that Duffy had concealed the role of the Trump administration's own modernization efforts.

Walkinshaw cited a September report from the Government Accountability Office warning that precisely this could happen.

“In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions," GAO said. "The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse—safety incidents.”

The fiasco prompted critics, including Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, to call for Duffy's resignation.

"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch," Hochul wrote on Facebook.

"Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency," she added, referring to the former MTV "Real World: Boston" and "Road Rules: All Stars" participant's "The Great American Road Trip" travel series, which features his family, including his wife, Fox News personality Rachel Campos Duffy.

The ground stop was the longest nationwide aviation shutdown in 25 years, with more than 3,500 aircraft already airborne when the FAA ordered the grounding. More than 4,100 flights were canceled Saturday alone, according to FlightAware.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that normal operations were expected to resume by Sunday evening.

item.title: Emacs Is My Browser (197 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://joshblais.com/blog/emacs-as-my-browser/, See on Hacker News

In my ever-increasing desire to use emacs as my sole computing environment, I have started to take browsing the web inside it far more seriously. Where I previously had thought EWW to be a niceity but far from capable, after using it for a few days it seems to be useable for about 85-90% of use cases - even on the javascript riddled hellhole that is the internet.

Why?#

I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).

In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.

The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.

Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:

I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.

How I am doing this#

For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.

I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.

Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page. Useful.

You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.

D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.

I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.

EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:

My browser.el setup:#

Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:

My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.

Limitations#

You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.

The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally. Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.

Conclusion#

I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.

As always, God bless, and until next time.

URL: https://jakub.jankiewicz.org/blog/ai-code-open-source/, See on Hacker News

This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers.

The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011:

The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes).

The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes).

zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes).

Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.)

item.title: A NES emulator written in Odin (111 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lucypero.com/lucynes.html, See on Hacker News

I made a NES emulator in Odin!

Github link

Intro

I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.

I’ve learned so much about:

  • The NES architecture, and possibly about game console architectures in general
  • Bits and bytes, hex notation, and bitwise operations.
  • The Odin programming language. I haven’t used it on a serious project before.
  • How computers work. CPU instructions, “cycles”, etc
  • Emulation. It’s very hard. Respect to emulator developers!

It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.

You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.

Features

  • Enough emulation accuracy to run Battletoads and hundreds of other games perfectly.
  • Debugger view with some debugging features
  • Menu view to interact with the emulator
  • Save states
  • Controller support
  • CRT Shader toggle
  • (Partial) Sound
  • Supported Mappers: NROM, MMC1, UXROM, CNROM, MMC3, GxROM, AxROM

Making an emulator

I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently, it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.

I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.

The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.

Another issue is mappers. Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.

Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.

The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:

  • The Nesdev wiki
  • The nesdev wiki discord. People here have helped me with my issues a lot.
  • Javidx’s NES series. The code has many mistakes but it’s a good starting point.
  • This article about the NES’s PPU
  • Test ROMS. These NES ROMS thoroughly test particular aspects of your emulator. This is an extraordinary tool to accelerate development of emulator accuracy.

I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.

Odin

I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.

One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion. When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer promotion.

One fun thing that I’ve learned was doing a bit of memory allocation strategy. Odin has no automatic memory management, so you have to come up with smart ways to handle memory. I’ve had fun thinking about how I should handle memory best. I didn’t need to do anything complicated. I mostly use one temporary allocator that clears every frame, a global heap allocator for things that need to live forever, and a NES Arena allocator for anything that needs to live along a NES session. I found memory allocation fun.

Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:

PpuCtrl :: struct #raw_union {
	// VPHB SINN
	using flags: bit_field u8 {
		n: u8 | 2,
		i: u8 | 1,
		s: u8 | 1, // sprite pattern table address for 8x8 sprites (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		b: u8 | 1, // bg pattern table address (0: $0000, 1: $1000)
		h: u8 | 1, // sprite size (0: 8x8, 1: 8x16)
		p: u8 | 1,
		v: u8 | 1, // vblank NMI enable
	},
	reg:         u8,
}

I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.

What’s missing

I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:

  • The sound. lucyNES doesn’t sound very well still. Some games will sound fine but most won’t. I have to improve the implementation, and implement the DMC channel which I haven’t done.
  • Some games that I’ve tested don’t work due to a poor mapper implementation
  • I could implement more mappers so more games are supported.

These are the main things that are lacking at this moment. Maybe at some point I will return and keep working on this so the project can feel “complete”.

item.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs (216 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings, See on Hacker News

This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

  • different positional methods in LLMs;

  • (finally) how RoPE works;

  • what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here, which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

  1. “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”

  2. “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub.)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)

Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.

If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.

We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information.

The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.

To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.

The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:

And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and xm the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is

Here,

  • Etoken is the embedding layer,

  • Pm is the position info vector selected by m,

  • and hm is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.

The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.

In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3]. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.

So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding Pm depends on the token’s own position m. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P2 and P7, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.

Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.

Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.

The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)

The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √(dmodel) before adding the position vectors, where dmodel is the embedding width.

So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formula

the formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is:

This scaling by √(dmodel) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical scales at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them.

In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same scale.

Now, the more interesting point is how the position embeddings Pm are computed.

Concretely, each position vector has the following entries:

As before, m denotes the position. The index i indexes a pair of features within the vector.

Here, a feature is one number in the position vector. For example, let’s assume we have a small vector with 8 values (dmodel = 8) that has entries numbered 0 through 7. (In the original paper this was 512 for the small model and 1024 for the bigger model, instead of 8, but that would be hard to visualize.) We group these into four pairs so that i goes from 0 through 3.

Here, the indices 2i and 2i + 1 select the two entries corresponding to pair i.

As shown in the equation earlier, the angle at position m, which is then fed into the sine or cosine functions to obtain Pm, 2i or Pm, 2i + 1, respectively, is computed as follows:

Figure 10 shows this calculation for all four pairs of our 8-feature example at position m = 2.

For an eight-feature embedding, the four frequencies are 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 radians per position. At position 2, the first pair in row 1 is (sin 2, cos 2) ≈ (0.909, −0.416).

The second pair, in row 2, changes more slowly, giving (sin 0.2, cos 0.2) ≈ (0.199, 0.980).

The figure below visualizes the sine and cosine calculations for different pairs, which are then collected in a position vector.

In short, this method is a (more complicated) alternative to obtaining positional embedding vectors compared to the GPT-2 method discussed earlier.

Similar to the GPT-2 embeddings, these are also absolute embeddings because each vector is computed from its own position. However, in contrast to the GPT-2 approach, the sine and cosine functions stay fixed during training. (Also, they can be extended and evaluated beyond the training positions, like beyond the context length of 1024, although that alone doesn’t guarantee that the model will perform well there, because it hasn’t seen those during training.)

To summarize, Figure 12 below compares the two ways of obtaining a position vector we discussed so far.

This sinusoidal method may look like an overly complicated way to obtain positional embeddings, however, understanding it will be useful when talking about RoPE in the next section.

Also, there is some rationale behind it. The authors chose sine and cosine because they make the shifting by a certain offset gives a certain deterministic difference. For example, the difference between position 2 to 5 and the difference between 102 to 105 is both 3, which then results in the same rotation.

According to the Attention Is All You Need paper:

“...easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos + k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.”

Or in less technical terms, the authors hypothesized that this property would make it easier for attention to learn relationships such as “three tokens earlier.”

Figure 13 below illustrates this for one sine/cosine pair. A rotation is a linear transformation, and both three-position shifts use the same rotation.

So, the sinusoidal method above is still considered an absolute positional encoding because the vector added to each token embedding represents that token’s position counted from the start of the sequence.

As shown in the previous figure, for example, tokens at positions 2 and 5 receive the position vectors P2 and P5. If we move those tokens to positions 102 and 105, they’re still three positions apart. But each token gets a different position vector because its absolute position m has changed.

So their attention score can change even when the token embeddings stay the same. The sinusoidal structure still gives the model a way to learn relative relationships.

Anyways, RoPE, which we will discuss below, builds this relative relationship directly into the attention calculation. RoPE, which Su et al. introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper, stands for Rotary Position Embedding and is considered a relative position method.

In attention, each token’s current representation is projected into a query, a key, and a value vector. Query-key dot products determine attention scores. After masking and softmax, the resulting weights determine how the value vectors are mixed. For a refresher, see my Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs article:

RoPE uses the token’s position to rotate its query and key vectors before their dot product. The value vectors bypass this rotation. Figure 14 below shows an overview of where RoPE is applied in a relatively recent MiniMax-M3, where QK-Norm normalizes queries and keys before RoPE.

As shown in the figure above, the LLM architecture has no explicit position vector added alongside the initial token embedding. Its explicit position signal is injected inside attention instead.

Side note: MiniMax-M3 rotates only part of each query and key head, a variation known as “partial RoPE” that we will cover later in Section 6.1. But to understand the basic RoPE operation first, let’s walk through the method step by step using a small example.

Attention usually divides its query, key, and value features into multiple heads, which are processed in parallel. Hence, the full mechanism is usually called Multi-head Attention (note that Grouped Query Attention also uses multiple heads). Here, each attention head computes its own attention scores and weighted sums. RoPE then acts on pairs of numbers within each query and key head.

To make this concrete, Figure 12 below follows a token representation through the learned query and key projections, which are computed via the weight matrices WQ and WK. In this toy example, each projection produces 16 features, which are reshaped into two heads with eight features each. In the figure below, every small cell contains one scalar feature, meaning one numerical entry in a vector (the numbers are not shown due to space reasons).

For the first eight-feature head, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], we pair each feature in the first half with the corresponding feature in the second half. This gives (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), and (4, 8). This split-half convention is used in LLM implementations, including my Qwen3 implementation. (We will compare it with the original, alternative adjacent-feature pairing method later after implementing the basic operation.)

Each pair gets a rotation angle determined by the token position m and that pair’s frequency θi. The corresponding query and key pairs use the same frequency. Figure 16 below shows how we rotate the pairs, put the updated features back in their original locations, and compute the query-key dot product.

The next section will walk through the figure(s) a bit more slowly.

For the following example, we’ll use the same two positions as before. The query comes from “the” at position m = 5, and the key comes from the first “fox” at position n = 2. Since, in this example, the key comes before the query, the causal mask allows the query to attend to it.

To illustrate the effect that the position has, and keeping everything fixed, let’s assume we start both pairs from the same two values, (1, 5).

Furthermore, for this example, let’s use θ = 20° per token position (π/9 radians per position). At position 2, we rotate the key’s arrow counterclockwise by 2 × 20° = 40°. At position 5, we rotate the query’s arrow by 5 × 20° = 100°.

To illustrate what’s happening in the figure above, for example, plugging cos 40° ≈ 0.766 and sin 40° ≈ 0.643 into the rotation from Figure 16 gives the new key coordinates:

Then, changing 40° to 100°, using the same equation as above, the rotated query pair becomes q′ ≈ (−5.098, 0.117). But the important point is that both arrows still have length √26. Only the rotation changes but the vectors keep the same lengths after the transformation.

For the key pair at position n, we use the same equations with nθ.

(Section 4 later shows how RoPE calculates the angular frequency for each feature pair.)

To close this section, for those more comfortable reading code, everything about RoPE illustrated so far can be written in code, as follows:

The resulting values are:

Original key:   (1, 5)

Rotated key:    (-2.448, 4.473)

If we rotate all 4 pairs in the 8-feature query (and key) vector(s), we get the vectors below. (We’ll come back to how we go from rotating one pair to rotating all of them later.)

Original key:   (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
Original query: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
